paper.abstract:
Abstract We consider the problem of binary sequence reconstruction where a sequence is transmitted multiple times over a channel, and each undergoes substitution errors by an arbitrary error vector of Hamming weight exactly t t .
We determine N wc N_{\mathrm{wc}} , the minimum number of distinct channel output observations guaranteeing unique reconstruction by an optimal decoder, and show that the bit-wise majority-vote decoder, which was proved by Levenshtein (2001) to be optimal for channels corrupting up to t t bits, is in fact suboptimal here.
Despite this suboptimality, we prove a condition that admits a practical early-termination rule, necessary for every decoder at any number of outputs N N , and sufficient for bit-wise majority-vote even below N wc N_{\mathrm{wc}} . We evaluate the number of outputs at which this condition is triggered, numerically, and show that it frequently occurs below N wc N_{\mathrm{wc}} when the block-length k > 2 ​ t + 1 k>2t+1 .
Finally, we propose an alternative algorithm aimed at guaranteeing unique reconstruction with fewer observations than bit-wise majority-vote, and demonstrate through exhaustive enumeration that it successfully decodes channel output-sets where bit-wise majority-vote fails.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: The problem of sequence reconstruction, first formalized by Levenshtein in [ 1 , 2 ] , addresses the recovery of an unknown sequence from multiple noisy channel output observations. The setup models settings in which redundancy introduced at the source might be insufficient for error-correction. Among other error types, Levenshtein determined the minimum number of distinct channel output observations required by any decoder to guarantee unique reconstruction when each observation is corrupted by up-to- t t substitution errors. Levenshtein also showed that the bit-wise majority-vote decoder is optimal, in that it successfully reconstructs given that many distinct observations. Since then, Levenshtein’s work was further extended in the case of deletion and insertion errors [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] , mixed error types [ 6 , 4 ] , coded settings [ 7 , 6 ] where the transmitted sequence belongs to a code, and list decoding [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] where the decoder may output multiple candidates. The works above establish worst-case guarantees under a combinatorial channel model, where the decoder must succeed given any set of sufficiently many channel outputs. A complementary line of work studies probabilistic channel models, e.g., [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] , where the goal is to determine how many channel output observations guarantee reconstruction with high probability. Recently, alternative perspectives have also emerged within Levenshtein’s combinatorial framework. In [ 15 , 16 ] , sufficient conditions for unique reconstruction that depend not only on the number of observations, but also on the pairwise distances among them are derived, enabling reconstruction with fewer observations than the worst-case threshold. A variant of Levenshtein’s channel, in which each observation is corrupted by exactly t t substitution errors, rather than at most t t , was introduced in [ 17 ] , where the average-case performance of the bit-wise majority-vote decoder was studied and bounds on the expected number of distinct noisy channel output observations needed for reconstruction under uniformly random constant-weight error patterns were derived. This model serves as a structured restriction of the classical up-to- t t model that renders the average-case analysis tractable. Beyond its analytical tractability, the exact- t t model is also motivated by settings where the error weight per observation is determined by a system-level constraint rather than a probabilistic mechanism, e.g., in adversarial scenarios where a jammer with a fixed corruption budget utilizes all available resources per transmission. In the present work, we study the worst-case behaviour of this exact- t t substitution channel and show that, perhaps surprisingly, the additional structure imposed by the fixed error weight renders the bit-wise majority-vote decoder suboptimal, thereby calling for the design of alternative reconstruction algorithms. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces necessary notation, relevant literature, and sets up the exact- t t substitution channel. Section III presents our results on bit-wise majority-vote suboptimality, by identifying the reconstruction-guarantee threshold, establishing a frequently encountered early-termination rule, and evaluating with representative parameters the performance gap between an optimal decoder and the bit-wise majority-vote decoder, which validates our claims. Section IV introduces a proposed weighted majority-vote decoder, studies its behaviour, and presents numerical evaluations supporting it as candidate decoder in regimes where bit-wise majority fails to reconstruct the transmitted sequence.

The bit-wise majority-vote decoder estimates each position of 𝐮 \mathbf{u} independently by selecting the value that appears most frequently at that position across N N observations. Position j j is decoded correctly when the column sum satisfies c j < N 2 c_{j}<\frac{N}{2} , since the majority of observations then agree on the correct value. IV Weighted Majority-Vote Decoders
sections.text: The suboptimality of the bit-wise majority-vote decoder established in Section III motivates the design of a low-complexity decoder that guarantees reconstruction with fewer than N maj N_{\mathrm{maj}} observations, perhaps even N wc N_{\mathrm{wc}} . Taking a step towards this goal, in this section we propose a weighted majority-vote decoder that exploits the exact- t t structure in an attempt to reduce the number of observations required below N maj N_{\mathrm{maj}} , at the cost of modest complexity increase. We first introduce the error-budget mechanism used in our suggested decoder construction (Section IV-A ). Our decoder, much like the majority-vote decoder, operates bit-wise; we observe that the order of decoding bits in our decoder is of paramount importance, and we hence aim to decode positions in decreasing order of “reliability”. We analyze the correctness of its first decision, as means of estimating its failure modes (Section IV-B ). Finally, we explain the order our construction uses, and formally present it (Section IV-C ). The performance of the decoder in comparison to bit-wise majority decoding is then numerically evaluated by exhaustive searches, where it is feasible to do so.

sections.heading: V Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper we revisit the exact- t t substitution error channel model and characterize its worst-case guarantee of unique reconstruction, for binary sequences. Using this result, we demonstrate that the bit-wise majority-vote decoder, proven by Levenshtein to be optimal in the up-to- t t scenario, is in fact suboptimal here. However, due to its simplicity, we devise an early-termination rule for the bit-wise majority-vote that applies even in cases where less than the worst-case required number of distinct channel output observations are available to the decoder. We then devise a weighted-majority decoder that exploits the correlations among errors in an attempt to improve the threshold of observations for unique reconstruction. This decoder comes with modest complexity increase, and outperforms simple bit-wise majority-vote decoding, numerically. We demonstrate the resulting performance increase of that decoder in a number of cases, which supports our (optimistic) conjecture that the suggested decoder indeed lowers the number of required observations to guarantee worst-case reconstruction.

Arvind Rameshwar , Antonia Wachter-Zeh , Abstract We consider the problem of binary sequence reconstruction where a sequence is transmitted multiple times over a channel, and each undergoes substitution errors by an arbitrary error vector of Hamming weight exactly t t . We determine N wc N_{\mathrm{wc}} , the minimum number of distinct channel output observations guaranteeing unique reconstruction by an optimal decoder, and show that the bit-wise majority-vote decoder, which was proved by Levenshtein (2001) to be optimal for channels corrupting up to t t bits, is in fact suboptimal here. Despite this suboptimality, we prove a condition that admits a practical early-termination rule, necessary for every decoder at any number of outputs N N , and sufficient for bit-wise majority-vote even below N wc N_{\mathrm{wc}} . We evaluate the number of outputs at which this condition is triggered, numerically, and show that it frequently occurs below N wc N_{\mathrm{wc}} when the block-length k > 2 ​ t + 1 k>2t+1 . Finally, we propose an alternative algorithm aimed at guaranteeing unique reconstruction with fewer observations than bit-wise majority-vote, and demonstrate through exhaustive enumeration that it successfully decodes channel output-sets where bit-wise majority-vote fails. Index Terms: Sequence reconstruction, fixed-weight substitution errors, bit-wise majority-vote decoding, early-termination. I Introduction The problem of sequence reconstruction, first formalized by Levenshtein in [ 1 , 2 ] , addresses the recovery of an unknown sequence from multiple noisy channel output observations. The setup models settings in which redundancy introduced at the source might be insufficient for error-correction. Among other error types, Levenshtein determined the minimum number of distinct channel output observations required by any decoder to guarantee unique reconstruction when each observation is corrupted by up-to- t t substitution errors. Levenshtein also showed that the bit-wise majority-vote decoder is optimal, in that it successfully reconstructs given that many distinct observations. Since then, Levenshtein’s work was further extended in the case of deletion and insertion errors [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] , mixed error types [ 6 , 4 ] , coded settings [ 7 , 6 ] where the transmitted sequence belongs to a code, and list decoding [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] where the decoder may output multiple candidates. The works above establish worst-case guarantees under a combinatorial channel model, where the decoder must succeed given any set of sufficiently many channel outputs. A complementary line of work studies probabilistic channel models, e.g., [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] , where the goal is to determine how many channel output observations guarantee reconstruction with high probability. Recently, alternative perspectives have also emerged within Levenshtein’s combinatorial framework. In [ 15 , 16 ] , sufficient conditions for unique reconstruction that depend not only on the number of observations, but also on the pairwise distances among them are derived, enabling reconstruction with fewer observations than the worst-case threshold. A variant of Levenshtein’s channel, in which each observation is corrupted by exactly t t substitution errors, rather than at most t t , was introduced in [ 17 ] , where the average-case performance of the bit-wise majority-vote decoder was studied and bounds on the expected number of distinct noisy channel output observations needed for reconstruction under uniformly random constant-weight error patterns were derived. This model serves as a structured restriction of the classical up-to- t t model that renders the average-case analysis tractable. Beyond its analytical tractability, the exact- t t model is also motivated by settings where the error weight per observation is determined by a system-level constraint rather than a probabilistic mechanism, e.g., in adversarial scenarios where a jammer with a fixed corruption budget utilizes all available resources per transmission. In the present work, we study the worst-case behaviour of this exact- t t substitution channel and show that, perhaps surprisingly, the additional structure imposed by the fixed error weight renders the bit-wise majority-vote decoder suboptimal, thereby calling for the design of alternative reconstruction algorithms. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces necessary notation, relevant literature, and sets up the exact- t t substitution channel. Section III presents our results on bit-wise majority-vote suboptimality, by identifying the reconstruction-guarantee threshold, establishing a frequently encountered early-termination rule, and evaluating with representative parameters the performance gap between an optimal decoder and the bit-wise majority-vote decoder, which validates our claims. Section IV introduces a proposed weighted majority-vote decoder, studies its behaviour, and presents numerical evaluations supporting it as candidate decoder in regimes where bit-wise majority fails to reconstruct the transmitted sequence.
